title: Rebuilding Your Identity and Self-Worth
subtitle: Rediscovering who you are after divorce
summary: **Divorce can shatter your sense of self.** You were someone's spouse, part of a couple, and now that identity is gone. This journey helps you rediscover who you are apart from your marriage, rebuild a healthy sense of self-worth that is not dependent on being chosen by another person, and step into a new chapter of life with confidence in who you are and whose you are.

cover.heroImageDescription: A person looking at their reflection with emerging confidence, symbolizing transformation and new identity.

targetOutcomes: Understand how divorce has affected your sense of identity
Separate your worth from your marital status
Rediscover your unique gifts passions and purpose
Build a healthy self-concept rooted in truth
Develop confidence independent of another person validation
Step into your future with a clear sense of who you are

activities.title: Who Am I Now? The Identity Crisis of Divorce
activities.subtitle: Understanding how divorce disrupts your sense of self
activities.whyThisMatters: Divorce creates an identity crisis. You were half of a couple, and now you are not. This activity helps you understand how divorce has affected your sense of self and why rebuilding identity is essential.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Major life transitions like divorce disrupt established identity and require intentional reconstruction.

cards.title: The Identity Disruption
cards.text:
**For years, your spouse was like a mirror reflecting back who you were.** Now that mirror is gone, and you find yourself asking: without that reflection, who am I?

**When Karen's divorce was finalized, she sat in her car and realized she did not know who she was anymore.**

**For fifteen years, she had been Mark's wife.** She introduced herself that way. Her social life revolved around being part of a couple. Her future was planned as part of a pair.

**Now she was just Karen.** But who was that? She had lost herself somewhere in the marriage, and now she had to figure out who she was on her own.

**This identity crisis is common after divorce.** You were someone's spouse. That role shaped how you saw yourself. Without it, you may feel lost, uncertain, or undefined.

cards.title: How Marriage Shapes Identity
cards.text:
**Marriage reshapes you in ways you do not notice until it is over.**

**You stopped being just you.** You became half of something. We instead of I. Our life instead of my life. At some point, you started using plural pronouns without thinking about it.

**You might have given up pieces of yourself along the way.** Hobbies that did not fit the marriage. Friends they did not like. Dreams that got put on hold and then forgotten. Parts of you that went underground because there was not room for them.

**You might have become someone different, someone shaped by the marriage itself.** The way their criticism made you smaller. The way their needs became more important than yours. The way you learned to manage their moods at the expense of knowing your own.

**Or maybe the marriage was good, and you simply grew together in ways that mean you cannot untangle where you end and where the we begins.**

Either way, divorce leaves you with a question you have not had to answer in years: Who am I without them? Who am I, just me, alone?

**That question is terrifying.** It is also an invitation.

cards.title: The Opportunity in Crisis
cards.text:
**Identity crisis is painful, but it is also an opportunity.**

**You get to decide who you want to be.** Not who your ex needed you to be. Not who you became in an unhealthy marriage. But who you actually are and want to become.

**This is a chance to rediscover parts of yourself that got lost.** To explore interests you set aside. To develop aspects of yourself that were neglected.

**Many people emerge from divorce knowing themselves better than before.** The painful process of rebuilding identity can lead to a stronger, more authentic sense of self.

**The crisis is real.** But so is the opportunity.

cards.title: Your Identity Experience
cards.text: How strongly has divorce affected your sense of identity?
prompts: Severely - I do not know who I am anymore
Significantly - Major parts of my identity feel disrupted
Moderately - Some aspects of my identity are shaken
Somewhat - I am adjusting but still feel uncertain
Mildly - My core sense of self remains mostly intact
I am actually discovering who I am for the first time

followUpLogic.reaction: Wherever you are, this journey will help you rebuild a strong healthy sense of who you are.

cards.title: Your Identity Questions
cards.text:
What questions are you asking about your identity since the divorce?

What parts of yourself feel lost or unclear? What roles or identities are you grieving? What do you wonder about who you are now? What aspects of yourself do you want to rediscover or develop?

Write about your identity questions:

cards.title: Embracing the Journey
cards.text:
**Commit to the identity rebuilding journey.**

**I acknowledge that my divorce has affected my sense of who I am.** I will not rush this process or pretend I have it all figured out. I will use this painful transition as an opportunity to discover who I truly am. I believe that a strong authentic identity is possible for me. I commit to doing the work to rebuild a healthy sense of self.

Write this commitment in your own words:

activities.title: Before and During: Who Were You in the Marriage?
activities.subtitle: Examining how you may have lost yourself
activities.whyThisMatters: To rebuild identity, it helps to understand what happened to it. This activity examines who you were before your marriage and how you may have changed or lost parts of yourself during it.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Understanding past identity helps reclaim lost aspects of self and build a more complete future identity.

cards.title: Before the Marriage
cards.text:
**Think back to who you were before your marriage.** Close your eyes for a moment. Who was that person?

What were your interests, hobbies, passions? What did you love to do? What excited you?

What were your friendships like? Who were you close to? What did your social life look like?

What were your dreams and goals? What did you want to accomplish? Where did you want to go?

What was your personality like? How did others describe you? What made you uniquely you?

**Some of these things may have continued into your marriage.** Others may have been lost along the way.

cards.title: How You Changed in Marriage
cards.text:
**Now think about who you became during the marriage.**

**Not who you were supposed to be.** Who you actually were.

Did you grow? Were there ways you expanded, became more yourself, flourished because of the relationship? Some marriages do that. They make both people bigger.

Or did you shrink? Did you become smaller, quieter, more careful? Did you lose access to parts of yourself that did not fit? Did you start to feel like you were performing a role instead of living a life?

Did you become someone you liked, or someone you barely recognize?

**Think about the person you were at the end of the marriage.** How much of that person was really you, and how much was adaptation to survive the relationship?

**This is not about blame.** Some changes were healthy. Some were necessary. But knowing which parts of your married self were authentic and which were accommodation helps you know what to keep and what to let go as you rebuild.

Who were you in that marriage? And how much of that person do you want to carry forward?

cards.title: What Got Lost
cards.text:
**Many people lose parts of themselves in marriage.**

**Interests get abandoned.** You stop doing things you loved because your spouse was not interested or did not approve.

**Friendships fade.** You drift from close friends as couple life takes over or as your spouse discourages those relationships.

**Dreams get shelved.** Your goals get subordinated to theirs or to the demands of the marriage.

**Voice gets silenced.** You stop expressing your opinions, needs, or feelings to avoid conflict.

**Identity gets absorbed.** You become so focused on being a spouse that you forget who you are apart from that role.

What got lost in your marriage that you want to reclaim?

cards.title: Your Before and During
cards.text:
**Reflect on who you were before and during your marriage.**

Who were you before you got married? What were your interests, relationships, dreams, personality? How did you change during the marriage? What healthy growth occurred? What unhealthy losses? What parts of yourself got lost or diminished?

Write about your before and during:

cards.title: What You Want to Reclaim
cards.text: What lost aspect of yourself do you most want to reclaim?
prompts: Dreams and goals I set aside
My voice and ability to express myself
Connection to who I really am

followUpLogic.reaction: Identifying what you want to reclaim helps focus your identity rebuilding efforts.

cards.title: One Step to Reclaim
cards.text:
**Choose one thing from your past self that you want to reclaim, and take a step toward it this week.**

**If you abandoned an interest, engage in it again.** If you lost a friendship, reach out to reconnect. If you stopped expressing yourself, share your real opinion about something. If you lost confidence, do something that challenges you.

What is one thing you will reclaim this week? What step will you take?

Write your reclaiming step:

activities.title: Worth Beyond Status: Separating Value from Being Chosen
activities.subtitle: Understanding that your worth is not determined by another person
activities.whyThisMatters: Divorce can devastate self-worth because rejection feels like proof that you are not valuable. This activity helps you separate your worth from whether another person chose you.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Human worth is intrinsic and not determined by relationship status or another person's choice.

cards.title: The Worth Wound
cards.text:
**There is a question underneath everything, the one you might be afraid to ask out loud.**

Am I worth less now?

**You used to be married.** Now you are divorced. In some circles, that feels like a demotion. Like you have been moved to a lower category of person. Less successful. Less chosen. Less worthy of respect.

**The question gets louder when you fill out forms.** Single, divorced, married. There it is in black and white. A checkbox that feels like a verdict.

**It gets louder when you see how people react.** The pity. The slight distance. The sense that you are now a cautionary tale instead of an equal.

**It gets louder in your own head.** The culture teaches that married is better. Whole. Complete. And you were married, and it failed, so what does that make you?

**Here is the truth that will take time to believe: your worth was never based on being married.** It is not based on being chosen by one particular person. It is not based on a relationship status.

**You had worth before marriage.** You had worth during marriage. You have worth now.

**Not because you earned it.** Because you exist. Because you are human. Because, if you believe Scripture, you are made in the image of God and loved by Him regardless of your marital status.

**The checkbox is not a verdict.** It is just a checkbox.

cards.title: Where Worth Actually Comes From
cards.text:
If worth does not come from being chosen by a spouse, where does it come from?

**True worth is intrinsic.** You have value simply because you exist. You are a human being made in the image of God. That gives you inherent dignity and worth.

**True worth is given by God.** He created you, loves you, and sent His Son for you. His valuation of you is the one that matters.

**True worth is not earned.** You do not become valuable by achieving, performing, or being chosen. You already are valuable.

**This means your worth was intact before marriage, during marriage, and after marriage.** It was never dependent on your spouse.

cards.title: The Lie of Being Unchosen
cards.text:
**Divorce plants a lie: You are unchosen.** Unwanted. Not enough.

**This lie is powerful because it taps into deep human fears.** We all want to be chosen, wanted, valued.

**But one person not choosing you does not make you unchosen.** Your ex is not the final authority on your worth. Their decision is about them, not a verdict on you.

**Furthermore, you are chosen.** Chosen by God before the foundation of the world. Chosen as His child. Chosen and loved.

**The lie says you are rejected.** The truth says you are beloved. Which voice will you believe?

cards.title: Your Worth Wounds
cards.text:
**Explore how divorce has affected your sense of worth.**

What lies about your worth have you believed since the divorce? How has rejection affected how you see yourself? In what ways have you felt not enough? What would change if you truly believed your worth was not determined by your ex?

Write about your worth wounds:

cards.title: Truths About Your Worth
cards.text:
Here are truths to counter the lies:

**You are made in God's image.** This gives you inherent dignity and worth. (Genesis 1:27)

**You are loved with an everlasting love.** God's love for you is not based on your performance or status. (Jeremiah 31:3)

**You are chosen and precious.** Before you did anything, God chose you. (1 (Peter 2:9)

**Your worth is not determined by your marital status.** Married people are not more valuable than single people.

**One person's rejection does not define your value.** Your ex does not have that authority.

**You are enough.** Not because you are perfect, but because you are His.

cards.title: Declaration of Worth
cards.text:
**Write and speak a declaration of your worth that does not depend on being chosen by another person.**

**My worth is not determined by my ex or by my marital status.** I am valuable because I am made in God's image and loved by Him. The rejection I experienced does not reduce my worth. My ex does not have authority over my value. I am chosen by God, beloved by Him, and precious in His sight. I will not believe the lie that I am not enough.

Write your declaration of worth in your own words:

activities.title: Uniquely You: Rediscovering Your Gifts and Strengths
activities.subtitle: Identifying what makes you uniquely valuable
activities.whyThisMatters: Part of rebuilding identity is rediscovering your unique gifts, strengths, and qualities. This activity helps you see what makes you distinctly you and valuable in ways that have nothing to do with your marriage.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Each person has unique gifts strengths and qualities that are part of their identity and value.

cards.title: Your Unique Design
cards.text:
**Rachel had forgotten she was good at anything.** Years of criticism had eroded her confidence until she could not remember what she used to enjoy or what she was capable of. One day, a friend asked her to help plan an event. To her surprise, she was good at it. Really good. Something long buried began to stir.

**You are not generic.** You are uniquely designed with specific gifts, strengths, personality traits, and qualities that no one else has in the same combination.

**These things existed before your marriage and exist after it.** They are not dependent on having a spouse.

**Divorce may have dimmed your awareness of these gifts.** You may have forgotten what you are good at. You may have lost confidence in your strengths.

**Part of identity rebuilding is rediscovering these unique aspects of who you are.** They have not disappeared. They just need to be uncovered again.

cards.title: Categories to Explore
cards.text:
**Consider these categories as you rediscover your uniqueness.**

Natural abilities: What are you naturally good at? What comes easily to you?

Learned skills: What have you developed through education and experience?

Personality strengths: What aspects of your personality are assets? Are you creative, analytical, compassionate, organized, adventurous?

Character qualities: What virtues do you possess? Honesty, perseverance, kindness, courage?

Passions: What do you care deeply about? What energizes you?

Experiences: What have you been through that has given you wisdom or perspective?

**You have more to offer than you may currently see.**

cards.title: What Others See
cards.text:
**Sometimes others see our gifts more clearly than we do.**

**Think about positive feedback you have received.** What have people thanked you for? What have you been complimented on? What do people come to you for help with?

**Think about what friends and family would say about your strengths.** If asked what is great about you, what would they say?

**Think about past accomplishments.** What have you achieved? What have you done well? What are you proud of?

**Your self-perception may be distorted by divorce.** Outside perspectives can help you see yourself more accurately.

cards.title: Your Unique Gifts
cards.text:
**Take time to identify your unique gifts and strengths.**

What are you naturally good at? What skills have you developed? What personality traits are strengths? What do others appreciate about you? What are you proud of having done or become?

List your unique gifts and strengths:

cards.title: Your Greatest Strength
cards.text: What do you think is your single greatest strength or gift?
prompts: Humor and ability to bring joy

followUpLogic.reaction: This strength is part of who you are regardless of your marriage. It contributes to your unique value.

cards.title: Using Your Gifts
cards.text:
**Your gifts are meant to be used.** Identify one way you will use a gift or strength this week.

**If you are compassionate, find someone to encourage.** If you are creative, make something. If you are good at organizing, tackle a project. If you are a good communicator, share your story.

**Using your gifts reinforces your sense of identity and worth.**

What gift will you use this week and how?

activities.title: What Lights You Up: Rediscovering Passions and Purpose
activities.subtitle: Finding what gives your life meaning and energy
activities.whyThisMatters: Identity includes knowing what you care about, what energizes you, and what gives your life meaning. This activity helps you rediscover or develop your passions and sense of purpose.

frameworkBasis.explanation: A clear sense of passion and purpose is central to a strong identity and meaningful life.

cards.title: Passion and Purpose
cards.text:
**Somewhere in you, there are things you love.** Things that light you up. Things you could lose yourself in for hours.

Do you remember what they are?

**Marriage can bury these things.** Sometimes because there was not time. Sometimes because your spouse did not share them. Sometimes because you forgot yourself in the work of being a couple.

What did you used to love before the marriage absorbed everything? What used to make you feel alive?

And what new things have you discovered, maybe even through the pain of divorce? Sometimes crisis reveals interests you did not know you had. Books that speak to you. Activities that calm you. Ways of being in the world that feel like coming home.

**Purpose is different from passion.** Passion is what you love. Purpose is why you are here.

**Some people have a clear sense of purpose.** Most are still figuring it out. And that is okay. You do not need a grand mission statement. You need something that gets you out of bed, something that makes you feel like your life matters.

**This is a time of rediscovery.** Not just finding yourself, but maybe finding parts of yourself that never got a chance to exist before. The you that is possible now that you have the space to become it.

What lights you up? What makes you feel like you are where you are supposed to be?

cards.title: Finding What Energizes You
cards.text:
**To rediscover your passions, pay attention to what energizes you.**

What activities make time fly? When do you lose yourself in engagement?

What topics fascinate you? What do you enjoy learning about?

What makes you feel alive? When do you feel most like yourself?

What did you love before your marriage that you stopped doing?

**Your passions may have been dormant, but they have not disappeared.** They are waiting to be rekindled.

**Giving yourself permission to pursue what you love is part of rebuilding identity.**

cards.title: Finding Your Why
cards.text:
**Purpose goes deeper than passion.** It is about meaning and contribution.

What breaks your heart about the world? What problems do you want to help solve?

What do you want your life to be about? When you reach the end, what will matter?

What unique contribution can you make? Given your gifts, experiences, and passions, what are you positioned to offer?

**Purpose does not have to be grand.** It can be raising good humans, bringing beauty into the world, caring for those who suffer, or simply loving people well.

**Knowing your why provides direction and meaning that transcends your circumstances.**

cards.title: Your Passions and Purpose
cards.text:
**Explore your passions and sense of purpose.**

What activities, topics, or pursuits energize you? What did you used to love that you want to return to? What do you care deeply about in the world? What do you want your life to be about?

Write about your passions and purpose:

cards.title: Permission to Pursue
cards.text:
**Give yourself permission to pursue what you love.**

**You may have spent years prioritizing others' interests.** You may feel guilty focusing on yourself. You may not think your passions matter.

**But pursuing your passions is not selfish.** It is part of becoming who you are meant to be. It fills you up so you have more to give.

**You do not need someone else's permission.** You do not need to justify it. You can choose to invest in what makes you come alive.

What would it look like to give yourself permission to pursue your passions?

cards.title: Pursuing Passion This Week
cards.text:
**Identify one passion or interest you will pursue this week.**

**It does not have to be big.** Read about something you find fascinating. Do an activity you love. Take a class. Join a group.

**The goal is to start rekindling what makes you come alive.**

What passion will you pursue this week? What specific step will you take?

activities.title: Who God Says You Are: Identity Rooted in Christ
activities.subtitle: Building your identity on the foundation that cannot be shaken
activities.whyThisMatters: The most stable foundation for identity is not what you do, what others think, or your relationships. It is who God says you are. This activity helps you build your identity on the unshakable foundation of your identity in Christ.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Biblical identity provides a stable foundation that does not depend on circumstances or human relationships.

cards.title: The Unstable and the Stable
cards.text:
**Some identity foundations are built on sand.** They feel solid until the storms come.

If your identity is based on your job, what happens when you lose it? If based on your appearance, what happens as you age? If based on your marriage, what happens in divorce?

**Identity built on things that can be taken away will always be vulnerable.**

**But there is a foundation that cannot be shaken: who you are in Christ.** This identity is not based on your performance, your relationships, or your circumstances. It is based on what God has done and who He says you are.

**Building on this foundation creates stability that survives life's storms, including divorce.**

cards.title: What God Says About You
cards.text:
**God sees you differently than you see yourself right now.**

**You look in the mirror and see failure.** He sees a child He loves.

**You feel defined by the divorce.** He defines you by whose you are, not what happened to you.

**You wonder if you are disqualified from good things.** He is preparing good things for you that you cannot yet imagine.

**This is not positive thinking.** It is not pretending the pain is not real. It is anchoring your identity in something that cannot be taken away.

**Your marriage could be taken away.** Your sense of yourself could be shattered. The life you planned could be destroyed.

But your standing with God? That cannot be stolen. It was never based on your performance in the first place. It was always, only, based on His love and Christ's work.

**Chosen.** Beloved. Adopted. Forgiven. These are not descriptions you have to earn. They are what is true about you because of who He is.

**The world says your divorce defines you.** God says your divorce is something that happened to you, not who you are.

Which voice will you believe?

cards.title: Living From Your True Identity
cards.text:
**Knowing your identity in Christ is one thing.** Living from it is another.

**Living from your true identity means reminding yourself of truth when lies attack.** When you feel worthless, you preach the gospel to yourself.

**It means making decisions based on who you are, not who you feel like.** Choosing to act like a beloved child of God even when you do not feel like one.

**It means finding your security in God's acceptance rather than human approval.** Not needing others to validate you because God already has.

**This takes practice.** But over time, your true identity becomes more real than false identities built on shakier ground.

cards.title: Your Identity Foundation
cards.text:
**Reflect on what your identity has been built on and what you want it to be built on.**

What have you based your identity on in the past? Marriage, career, appearance, achievement? How has divorce exposed the instability of those foundations? How firmly is your identity rooted in who God says you are?

Write about your identity foundation:

cards.title: Anchoring in Truth
cards.text:
**To build identity on Christ, anchor yourself in truth.**

**Meditate on Scripture that reveals your identity.** Let these truths sink deep into your heart and mind.

**Speak truth to yourself.** When lies come, counter them with what God says about you.

**Pray your identity.** Thank God for who He has made you. Ask Him to help you live from that reality.

**Surround yourself with reminders.** Write verses on cards. Put them where you will see them. Let truth surround you.

**Identity reconstruction happens through repetition of truth over time.**

cards.title: Identity Anchoring Practice
cards.text:
**Choose one identity truth from Scripture to anchor yourself in this week.**

I am a child of God (John 1:12) I am loved unconditionally (Romans 8:39) I am forgiven completely (Psalm 103:12) I am chosen and precious (1 (Peter 2:9) I am a new creation (2 (Corinthians 5:17) I am God's masterpiece (Ephesians 2:10)

**Write the verse on a card.** Read it every morning and evening. When lies attack, speak this truth.

Which truth will you anchor in this week?

activities.title: Rewriting Your Story: Creating a New Narrative
activities.subtitle: Moving from victim story to growth story
activities.whyThisMatters: The story you tell yourself about your divorce shapes your identity. This activity helps you craft a narrative that acknowledges the pain while also making room for growth, redemption, and a hopeful future.

frameworkBasis.explanation: The stories we tell about ourselves shape our identity and our sense of possibility.

cards.title: The Power of Narrative
cards.text:
**You are both the author and the main character of your life story.** Divorce wrote a painful chapter you did not choose. But the pen is back in your hand now. What happens next is yours to write.

**The story you tell about your divorce shapes who you become.**

**If your story is I am a victim who was wronged and will never recover, that shapes your identity one way.**

**If your story is I went through something painful and I am becoming stronger and wiser through it, that shapes your identity differently.**

**Both stories may contain truth.** You may have been wronged. You may also be growing. The question is which narrative becomes primary.

**You are not just a passive recipient of your story.** You have the power to shape how you understand and tell it.

cards.title: Unhelpful Narratives
cards.text:
**Some narratives keep you stuck.**

**The pure victim story says this was done to me and I had no part in it.** While you may have been genuinely wronged, staying in pure victim mode prevents growth.

**The pure shame story says this is all my fault and proves I am worthless.** This narrative denies the complexity of what happened and destroys self-worth.

**The hopeless story says my life is ruined and good things are not possible anymore.** This narrative closes off the future.

**The bitter story says I will never forgive and will carry this anger forever.** This narrative traps you in the past.

**These narratives may feel true, but they are incomplete and ultimately harmful.**

cards.title: A Redemptive Narrative
cards.text:
**A redemptive narrative acknowledges the pain while making room for growth.**

**It is honest about what happened: I went through a painful divorce.** It was hard and I was hurt.

**It takes appropriate responsibility: I contributed to some problems.** I have learned from my mistakes.

**It refuses to be defined by the pain: My divorce is part of my story, not my whole story.**

**It looks for meaning and growth: I am becoming stronger, wiser, more compassionate through this.**

**It stays open to the future: Good things are still possible.** My best days may still be ahead.

**This is not pretending.** It is choosing which truths to emphasize.

cards.title: Your Current Narrative
cards.text:
**Examine the narrative you have been telling yourself about your divorce.**

What story do you tell about what happened? Is it primarily a victim story, shame story, hopeless story, or something else? How is this narrative affecting your identity and future? What would a more redemptive narrative sound like?

Write about your current narrative:

cards.title: Crafting Your New Story
cards.text:
**You can intentionally craft a new narrative about your divorce.**

**Start with honesty.** Acknowledge what happened and how it hurt.

**Take ownership of your part without excessive self-blame.**

**Identify what you are learning and how you are growing.**

**Name the strengths that are emerging through the difficulty.**

**Express hope for what lies ahead.**

**This new story does not deny the pain.** It places the pain in a larger context that includes redemption and possibility.

cards.title: Writing Your Redemptive Story
cards.text:
**Write a brief redemptive narrative of your divorce experience.**

**Include what happened, what you have learned, how you are growing, and what you hope for the future.**

**Example: I went through a painful divorce after my spouse was unfaithful.** It devastated me, and I struggled with anger and self-doubt. But I am learning to trust God more deeply, to value myself apart from a relationship, and to be more discerning. I am stronger than I knew. I believe good things are still ahead for me.

Write your redemptive story:

activities.title: Standing Tall: Rebuilding Confidence
activities.subtitle: Developing confidence that does not depend on a relationship
activities.whyThisMatters: Divorce often devastates confidence. You may doubt yourself, your judgment, and your ability to navigate life alone. This activity helps you rebuild confidence that comes from within rather than from a relationship.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Confidence can be rebuilt through small wins, skill development, and changing self-talk.

cards.title: The Confidence Collapse
cards.text:
**Divorce can collapse confidence in several ways.**

**You may doubt your judgment.** You chose this person. You did not see the problems. How can you trust your decisions now?

**You may doubt your lovability.** If they did not want you, maybe no one will.

**You may doubt your competence.** You are now handling things alone that you used to share. Can you really do this?

**You may doubt your future.** If this happened, what else might go wrong?

**This confidence collapse is normal after divorce.** But it does not have to be permanent. Confidence can be rebuilt.

cards.title: Where Confidence Comes From
cards.text:
**Healthy confidence comes from several sources.**

**Competence builds confidence.** When you develop skills and accomplish things, confidence grows.

**Experience builds confidence.** When you face hard things and survive, you learn you can handle difficulty.

**Identity builds confidence.** When you know who you are and whose you are, you have a stable foundation.

**Self-talk builds confidence.** The things you say to yourself either build up or tear down your confidence.

**Notice that none of these sources requires a romantic relationship.** You can be confident without being coupled. Confidence comes from within, not from someone else choosing you.

cards.title: Rebuilding Strategies
cards.text:
**Several strategies help rebuild confidence.**

**Collect small wins.** Accomplish things. Complete tasks. Each win builds momentum.

**Develop competence.** Learn new skills. Become capable in areas where you relied on your spouse.

**Face fears.** Do things that scare you. Proving you can handle challenges builds confidence.

**Change your self-talk.** Replace critical inner voice with encouraging truth. Speak to yourself like a coach, not a critic.

**Remember past successes.** You have accomplished things before. You have handled hard things. You can do it again.

**Take care of yourself.** When you look and feel your best, confidence follows.

cards.title: Your Confidence Assessment
cards.text:
**Assess your current confidence.**

Where has your confidence been most damaged by divorce? What areas of life do you feel most insecure about? What would you attempt if you had more confidence? What has built your confidence in the past?

Write about your confidence assessment:

cards.title: Your Confidence Priority
cards.text: What area most needs confidence rebuilding?
prompts: Trusting my own judgment and decisions
Believing I am lovable and valuable
Social confidence and meeting new people

followUpLogic.reaction: Focus your confidence rebuilding efforts in this area first.

cards.title: Your Confidence Building Plan
cards.text:
**Create a plan to rebuild confidence.**

**One small win I will accomplish this week.**

**One skill I will develop that builds competence.**

**One fear I will face that scares me.**

**One way I will change my negative self-talk.**

Write your confidence building plan:

activities.title: A New Chapter: Stepping Into Your Future Self
activities.subtitle: Envisioning and becoming who you want to be
activities.whyThisMatters: Identity rebuilding is not just about recovering the past. It is about becoming who you want to be in the future. This activity helps you envision your future self and take steps toward becoming that person.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Envisioning and moving toward a desired future self is a powerful part of identity formation.

cards.title: Beyond Recovery
cards.text:
**Identity rebuilding is not just about getting back to who you were.** It is about becoming who you want to be.

**You are not the same person you were before your marriage.** You have been through something significant. You have learned things, developed strengths, and gained perspective you did not have before.

**This is an opportunity not just to recover lost parts of yourself but to become a new, better version of who you are.**

What kind of person do you want to become? Who do you want to be in this new chapter of your life?

cards.title: Envisioning Your Future Self
cards.text:
**Two years after his divorce, Marcus barely recognized himself, and for the first time, that was a good thing.** He was healthier, more self-aware, kinder to himself. The divorce had nearly destroyed him. But in rebuilding, he had become someone he actually liked.

**Imagine yourself one year from now, or five years from now, having done the work of healing and growth.**

What does that person look like? How do they carry themselves? What confidence do they have?

How do they spend their time? What relationships do they have? What are they doing with their life?

How do they think about themselves? What do they believe about their worth? How do they handle difficulty?

What character qualities do they have? What strengths have they developed?

**This future self is not fantasy.** It is possibility. And you can become that person.

cards.title: Becoming Your Future Self
cards.text:
**You become your future self through small daily choices.**

**Act as if.** Begin acting like the person you want to become, even before you feel like it. Behavior often precedes feelings.

**Make choices aligned with your future self.** When facing decisions, ask what would my best future self do?

**Develop habits that shape you.** The person you become is largely shaped by what you do daily.

**Surround yourself with people who call out the best in you.** Community shapes identity.

**Practice becoming.** Identity is not fixed. You are always becoming. Be intentional about what you are becoming.

cards.title: Your Future Self
cards.text:
**Describe your future self in detail.**

Who do you want to be one year from now? Five years from now? What qualities do you want to have? How do you want to live? What do you want to be known for? What would make you proud of who you have become?

Write a description of your future self:

cards.title: The Gap and the Bridge
cards.text:
**There is a gap between who you are now and who you want to become.** That gap is not a problem. It is normal.

**The bridge across the gap is built one step at a time.** Each choice that aligns with your future self narrows the gap.

**You do not have to become your future self overnight.** You just need to take the next step.

What is one step you could take today that would move you toward becoming the person you want to be?

**Small steps, taken consistently, lead to transformation.**

cards.title: Steps Toward Your Future Self
cards.text:
**Identify specific steps to move toward your future self.**

**One habit I will develop that shapes me toward who I want to become.**

**One choice I will make differently, aligned with my future self.**

**One relationship I will nurture that calls out the best in me.**

**One thing I will stop doing that holds me back from becoming who I want to be.**

Write your steps toward your future self:

activities.title: Knowing Who You Are: Your Identity Commitment
activities.subtitle: Committing to living from your true identity
activities.whyThisMatters: You have done significant work in understanding and rebuilding your identity. This activity helps you consolidate that work and commit to living from your true identity going forward.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Identity reconstruction requires ongoing commitment to living from truth rather than old patterns.

cards.title: What You Have Explored
cards.text:
**Through this journey, you have done important identity work.**

**You have examined how divorce affected your sense of self.** You have explored who you were before and during your marriage. You have separated your worth from your marital status.

**You have rediscovered your unique gifts and passions.** You have grounded your identity in who God says you are. You have begun rewriting your story.

**You have started rebuilding confidence and envisioning your future self.**

**This is significant work.** You now have a clearer sense of who you are than you did before.

cards.title: Identity Is Ongoing
cards.text:
**Identity is not something you figure out once and then you are done.** It is ongoing.

**There will be days when old lies return.** Days when you forget who you are. Days when rejection or failure makes you question your worth.

**On those days, return to what you have learned.** Remind yourself of truth. Practice the disciplines of identity.

**Identity solidifies over time through consistent choices to live from truth rather than lies.** Keep choosing.

**You are not who you were.** You are becoming who God made you to be.

cards.title: Your Key Identity Insight
cards.text:
What is the most important thing you have learned or realized about your identity through this journey?

What do you want to remember when you forget who you are?

Write your key identity insight:

cards.title: Your Identity Statement
cards.text:
**Write a personal identity statement that captures who you are.**

**Include your worth, your unique gifts, your passions, and your identity in Christ.**

**Example: I am a beloved child of God, valuable not because of my marital status but because He made me and loves me.** I am creative, compassionate, and strong. I am passionate about helping others and creating beauty. I am becoming someone who walks in confidence and purpose.

Write your identity statement:

cards.title: A Prayer for Identity
cards.text:
**Father, thank You for who You have made me to be.**

**Thank You that my identity is not determined by my ex, my divorce, or my marital status.** It is determined by You.

**Help me live from my true identity as Your beloved child.** When lies attack, remind me of truth. When I forget who I am, bring me back to You.

**I am Yours.** I am loved. I am chosen. I am valuable. I have a purpose.

**Help me walk in the confidence of who You say I am.**

**In Jesus' name, Amen.**

cards.title: Your Identity Commitment
cards.text:
**Make a commitment to living from your true identity.**

**I commit to believing what God says about me over what lies tell me.**

**I commit to pursuing my passions and using my gifts.**

**I commit to building confidence through action and truth.**

**I commit to becoming the person I want to be, one choice at a time.**

**I know who I am.** I am walking into my future with clarity and confidence.

Sign your commitment and write your next step:

journeyCompletionSummary.summaryText: You have done significant work in rebuilding your sense of identity and self-worth. You now have a clearer picture of who you are apart from your marriage, grounded in truth rather than lies. Continue to live from your true identity, and remember that you are beloved, valuable, and purposed regardless of your relationship status.
keyTakeaways: Divorce disrupts identity but creates opportunity for rediscovery
Parts of yourself lost in marriage can be reclaimed
Your worth is not determined by being chosen by another person
You have unique gifts and strengths that define your value
Passions and purpose give meaning beyond relationships
Identity rooted in Christ provides stable foundation
You can rewrite your narrative from victim story to growth story
Confidence can be rebuilt through small wins and changed self-talk
You are not just recovering but becoming your future self
